senses: One who commits rape; a rapist.
ety: From rape + -er.
examples: Rosa refused to return to the lair of the raper, but was induced to give Tudy what his mother described as ‘his last bit of happiness’ in a bower hastily got ready at Montrose, the La Plante mansion on Greenock Heights.

senses: One who believes in the existence of a god or gods.
ety: From Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”) + English -ist.
examples: The term stands in contradistinction to theism which, in its widest sense, means belief in a personal god, goddess, gods and /or goddesses.
No one is to be called a Theist, who does not believe in a Personal God, whatever difficulty there may be in defining the word "Personal."

senses: The rectangular great hall in a Mycenaean building, usually supported with pillars.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μέγαρον (mégaron).
examples: The megaron is a hall building with an open-fronted porch, but this porch is not just any laterally confined space.

senses: Any drain cleaner.
ety: Appellativization from the Drāno brand by S. C. Johnson & Son, constructed from drain + -o.
examples: Farnsworth: they'll burrow so deep into the bowel that not even Hermes' famous Jerk Prunes could dislodge them! Hermes: I call it Caribbean Draino.

senses: To lay (something) underneath something else; to put under.
To provide a support for something; to raise or support by something laid under.
To put a tap on (a shoe).
To incline from the vertical.
ety: From Middle English underleyen, from Old English underleċġan (“to underlay, prop, support”), equivalent to under- + lay. Cognate with Dutch onderleggen (“to lay or put under”), German unterlegen (“to underlay”), Swedish underlägga (“to underlay”).
examples: We underlaid the carpet with felt.

senses: To demarcate.
ety: From French démarquer, from New Latin *demarcō (“to mark off, set the bounds of, bound”), from Latin dē- (“off”) + Medieval Latin marcō (“to mark”), from marca (“bound, mark, march”). By surface analysis, de- + mark. See mark, march.
examples: The book's three sections: "An Accidental Childhood," "A Feminine Age," and "The Wider Sphere Of Reference" — demark the familial, social and personal landscapes which Strouse carefully maps out.

senses: A lessening, decrease or reduction.
The act or process of making diminutive.
a compositional technique where the composer shortens the melody by shortening its note values.
ety: From Middle English diminucioun, from Anglo-Norman diminuciun, Old French diminucion, from Latin dīminūtiō.
examples: The new emission standards have produced a measurable diminution in air pollution.
Another part, feeling a diminution of confidence in him, still hope that the general tenor of his conduct will be essentially right.
Cold is usually shapeless, I suppose, extending over large spaces equally, or with gradual diminution.

senses: To play (a radio, recorded music, etc.) at extremely loud volume levels.
To express (ideas, words, etc.) loudly; to proclaim.
To make a loud sound, especially like a trumpet.
ety: The verb is derived from Late Middle English blaren, bleren, bloren (“to bellow, cry, wail; of a goat: to bleat”), probably from Old English *blǣran, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁- (“to bleat, cry”) and ultimately imitative. Related to Middle Dutch blaren, bleren (“to bawl, cry; to shout; to bleat”) (modern Dutch blèren). The noun is derived from the verb. Cognates German Low German blaren, blarren Middle High German blêren, blerren (modern German plärren) Saterland Frisian blärje West Frisian blearje
examples: The trumpet blaring in my ears gave me a headache.
Blazon your mottos of blessing and prayer! / Welcome her, welcome her, all that is ours! / Warble, O bugle, and trumpet, blare! / Flags, flutter out upon turrets and towers!

senses: The position of a human figure whose hips and legs are twisted away from the direction of the head and shoulders; (countable) an instance of this.
ety: Borrowed from Italian contrapposto (“contrasting; opposing”, adjective), the past participle of contrapporre (“to set against, counter”), from Latin contrāpōnere, the present active infinitive of contrāpōnō (“to oppose; to place opposite”), from contrā (“against; contrary to”) + pōnō (“to place, put”). The plural form contrapposti is borrowed from Italian contrapposti, the masculine plural form of contrapposto.
examples: The hawkers' athletic contrappostos, intellectual and imaginary rather than plausible, speak of the mind's superiority to the body.

senses: Associated with spinning; moving with a spinning motion.
ety: From spin + -y. Noun sense 1 (“hard drive”) is an allusion to disk platters spinning inside a hard drive while powered on.
examples: Then you got a double whammy - your eyes were full of orange and your head was spinny and dizzy.

senses: The Eucharist, when given to a person who is dying or one in danger of death.
Provisions, money, or other supplies given to someone setting off on a long journey.
A portable altar.
ety: From Latin viāticum (“travelling-money, provisions for a journey”), from viāticus (“of a road or journey”), from via (“road”). Doublet of voyage.
examples: Towards night-fall he entered a town called Sa’adiyah where he alighted and took out somewhat of his viaticum and ate.
That viaticum I had been made to drink had undoubtedly been spiked with cantharides or something.

senses: To make rough.
To become rough.
ety: From rough + -en.
examples: The wind began to roughen the surface of the sea.
They roughened the edges of the stone to give it a rustic look.

senses: A Japanese food made by putting ingredients into white rice, wrapping the outside with laver, and shaping it into a triangle.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese お握り (onigiri).
examples: He cooks his breakfast of rice and misoshiru and packs onigiri rice balls for his lunch.

senses: Netted: made of or employing a net.
ety: From net (“openwork fabric mesh”) + -y (“forming adjectives”).
examples: Ye ought for to keepe them close, till the day haue taken the gellie or netty rime, from the earth.

senses: Resembling, containing, or composed of calcium carbonate or limestone; chalky.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin calcārius (“of or pertaining to lime”), derived from calx (“lime”). Similar to calcium.
examples: Instead, the spoil will be used in part to create 127 hectares of new calcareous grassland (alkaline grassland), woodland, wood pasture, and wetland habitats.

senses: A curtain; a drapery.
The way in which fabric falls or hangs.
A member of a youth subculture distinguished by its sharp dress, especially peg-leg pants (1950s: e.g. Baltimore, MD). Antonym: square.
A dress made from an entire piece of cloth, without having pieces cut away as in a fitted garment.
ety: From Middle English drape (“a drape”, noun), from Old French draper (“to drape; to full cloth”), from drap (“cloth, drabcloth”), from Late Latin drappus, drapus (“drabcloth, kerchief”), a word first recorded in the Capitularies of Charlemagne, probably from Frankish *drapi, *drāpi (“that which is fulled, drabcloth”, literally “that which is struck or for striking”), from Proto-Germanic *drapiz (“a strike, hit, blow”) and Proto-Germanic *drēpiz (“intended for striking, to be beaten”), both from *drepaną (“to beat, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreb- (“to beat, crush, make or become thick
examples: The herringbone-twill sample is soft and smooth, with an easy drape that allows the fabric to move beautifully.

senses: Anything awkwardly large or unwieldy.
ety: First attested 1813, from translingual Mastodon (1806), coined by French naturalist Georges Cuvier, from masto- (“breast”) + -odon (“tooth”), due to the mammilloid (“nipple-shaped”) projections on the crowns of the extinct mammal's molars.
examples: The battery is dying, and Natalia's iPhone charger doesn't fit my mastodon of a phone anyway.
Nor does it work for governance: the policy has become such a mastodon that we can't adapt it quickly enough to different regions or different circumstances.

senses: In favour of recreational drugs.
ety: From pro- (“favouring”) + drug.
examples: In France, the antidrug law forbids all forms of prodrug propaganda.

senses: A genre of Japanese fiction involving everyday people transported to alternative fantasy or virtual worlds.
A genre of Japanese fiction in which the protagonist is reincarnated.
Any piece of media in the above genres.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 異世界 (isekai, literally “different world”).
examples: It's not every day that an isekai author gets published out of the sea of isekai stories on there.

senses: The belief in, or practice of, living without food, subsisting instead on prana or sunlight.
ety: From breatharian + -ism.
examples: Wiley Brooks, the guru of Breatharianism, espouses a system of physical vitality by which one may stop eating and drinking entirely, and live, lichenlike, off light and air.
Followers of the cult Breatharianism believe that the energy they save on digesting food and drink can be transformed into physical, emotional and spiritual energy.

senses: A sweet, stretchable chewing gum designed for blowing bubbles.
A light pink colour, the hue in which bubblegum is traditionally coloured.
ety: From bubble + gum.
examples: Kim—tanned, a bubblegum-pink mouth, pegged jeans, high butt, high heels.

senses: The small, triangular, edible nut of the beech tree.
ety: From beech + nut.
examples: The cultivated harvest in the fields was matched by the woodland ‘mast’ of beechnuts, acorns, chestnuts, and other fruits of the forest.

senses: Any of several medium to large flies, of the family Tabanidae, that suck the blood of mammals (not to be confused with Stomoxys calcitrans, the stable fly, or dog fly).
ety: From Middle English horse fliȝe, equivalent to horse + fly.
examples: It was not a horsefly and it was not a deerfly; it was bigger than either.

senses: To wail over; to feel or express deep sorrow for.
ety: From Middle English bewailen, equivalent to be- (“over, about”) + wail.
examples: And all wept, and bewailed her: but he said, Weep not; she is not dead, but sleepeth.
Far from bewailing the existence of mysteries-for-humans, we should be extremely grateful for it.

senses: The liquid left over from boiling chickpeas or similar beans, or from a can of chickpeas.
ety: Coined by US software engineer Goose Wohlt in 2015, from Latin aqua (“water”) + faba (“bean”).
examples: Soybean and chickpea aquafabas are particularly thick (think about the goo in canned chickpeas), but any bean water.

senses: Silly or scatterbrained, usually of a young woman.
ety: Since early 1800s commonly used by Pennsylvania Dutch (Penslfawnisch Deitsch); possibly a borrowing from dialectal German dutzig, also dützig, ditzig (“numb, dazed, dizzy, as after having been punched; dull, stupid”), from dialectal dutzen (“to butt, hit, punch”). Compare German verdutzt (“dumbfounded”) and regional Dötsche (“bump, dent, bruise”). Unlikely, an alteration of dizzy, of American origin.
examples: The guy tossed some cash on the counter, then left with the ditzy girl and Abigail's fan.

After hiring a crew of young guys and gals including loyal Jo, unlucky-in-love Frankie, strapping Bob, wisecracking Dee Dee, ditzy blonde Jonesy and titian-haired Penny, the gang drives up to the lodge.

senses: Overly patriotic or nationalistic, often with an element of favouring war or an aggressive foreign policy.
ety: From jingo + -istic.
examples: My editorial angered both the jingoistic war hawks and the anti-war protesters.
All this jingoistic bombast, however, was directed toward defending, not so much the national vernacular as the national belles lettres.
But are these Olympics also destined to become a jingoistic, flag-waving convention, a world-alienating Patriot Games?

senses: The process of stripping hair from the skin so as to make it smooth; unhairing; hair removal.
The removal of hair, wool or bristles from the body.
ety: From depilate + -ation.
examples: Hair had appeared in greater quantities where I didnʼt want it, and I couldnʼt keep up with the demands of depilation.

senses: A noisy celebration or party; also, an evening of traditional music and dance.
Chiefly in the form to blow a hooley: a strong wind; a gale.
ety: The etymology of sense 1 (“noisy celebration or party”) is unknown. Sense 2 (“strong wind”) is possibly from one of the following: * Borrowed from Orkney Scots hool(an) (“strong wind”) + English -ie (diminutive suffix). Hoolan is derived from Norn (unattested), from Old Norse ýlun (“howling, wailing”), from ýla (“to howl”) (ultimately onomatopoeic) + -un (suffix forming nouns). * From sense 1.
examples: At a family gathering, a wake or a Christmas hooley, other children would step forward to sing a rhyme or dance a hornpipe.
The celebratory ceilidh at the Culag Hotel in Lochinver is still talked about. 'Oh, it was a fine evening,' one discreet woman said to me. 'A right damn wild hoolie!' a well-oiled friend enthused.
She had always loved what she called a hooley, a gathering of family and friends, and her dying was to be her last, greatest hooley.

senses: To be part of a clade; to form a clade.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κλάδος (kládos, “shoot, branch”). Coined by British evolutionary biologist, philosopher, author Julian Huxley in 1957 in a paper titled The Three Types of Evolutionary Process in Nature. Doublet of cladus and possibly holt.
examples: The phylogenetic tree for CiCBR shows it clades with the human cannabinoid receptors rather than with those other human GPCRs which most closely resemble the cannabinoid receptors.

senses: Of a person or animal, or their behaviour: calm and composed (often in a dignified manner), and avoiding or unaffected by activity or excitement.
Of an object, particularly a building: not overly ornate or showy; not having a strong colour or design.
Of writing: not emotional; calm, composed.
ety: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English sedate (“not painful or sore”), and directly from its etymon Latin sēdātus (“calm, quiet, composed”), participial adjective from sēdō (“to allay, appease, calm, settle; to end, stop”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”). Compare English -ate (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘characterized by [the thing specified]’). The verb is partly derived from sēdāt-, a participial stem of sēdō (verb sense 2—“to make (someone or something) calm”; see above), and partly a back-formation from sedation (verb sense 1—“to give (a person) a se
examples: A reel or fling of some sort was in progress; and the usually sedate Farfrae was in the midst of the other dancers in the costume of a wild Highlander, flinging himself about and spinning to the tune.
Then she saw that they were waving their handkerchiefs; dipping them up and down, with a curiously sedate, formal motion.
Facing the Parliament Buildings across James’ Bay arose a sedate stone and cement Post Office.

senses: To adapt something to the needs or tastes of an individual.
To represent something abstract as a person; to embody.
To imbue something with one's personality.
ety: From personal + -ize.
examples: Gloria Hull, best known as a Black Feminist literary critic, expands and personalizes her examination of creative thought in her first collection of poetry, Healing Heart.

senses: A piece of armor for the hips and thighs: one of a set of plates (each being of one piece or segmented) hanging from the bottom of the breastplate or from faulds.
ety: Inherited from Middle English tasse (“armor plate protecting the hip”), derived from Old French tasse, tasche (“purse; pouch”), derived from Frankish *taskā (“pouch”), derived from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ. Cognate with Old High German tasca (“pouch”), German Tasche (“pocket; pouch; bag”), Dutch tas (“bag”).
examples: The tasse, meant only to cover the hips, was so long that its edges scraped against the floor.

senses: Implied, but not made explicit, especially through silence.
ety: Borrowed from late Middle French tacite, or from Latin tacitus (“that is passed over in silence, done without words, assumed as a matter of course, silent”), from tacere (“to be silent”).
examples: Our tacit treaty with Miss Maudie was that we could play on her lawn, eat her scuppernongs if we didn’t jump on the arbor, and explore her vast back lot,
He does this by way of a tacit reference to Homer.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a troll (supernatural being).
Resembling or characteristic of a troll (Internet troublemaker) or trolling.
ety: From troll + -ish.
examples: Clara's father, a trollish ne'er-do-well who spent most of his time in brothels and saloons, would disappear for days and weeks at a stretch, leaving Clara and her mother to fend for themselves.
If you get a “trollish” comment, delete it, do not respond to it, and move forward immediately without paying any further mind.

senses: Someone who actively prepares for emergencies by having useful things on hand, such as extra water, food, medicine, fuel, and so on.
A survivalist.
ety: From prep (“prepare”, verb) + -er.
examples: The preppers were living in flush times in a beautiful region, but it seemed like the first thing they did with money was steel for the apocalypse.

senses: A sheep of a Spanish breed with long, fine hair.
The wool of this sheep.
The fabric made from this wool (or from any similar yarn).
A dress made out of merino fabric.
A yarn made from a combination of wool and cotton in imitation of this wool.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish merino.
examples: The experimental farm has pure merinos, German merinos and new Dorsians, but it is not yet decided what experimental work will be undertaken.
The Priest pulled the light merino carriage rug higher about his knees.

senses: A community of bards, usually Welsh, but sometimes Breton or Cornish.
ety: From Welsh gorsedd (“throne”), itself a compound of gor- (“super-, over-”) + sedd (“seat”).
examples: Now a Gorsedd is a competition for Bardic honours.

senses: An electronic device for connecting a balanced transmission line to an unbalanced one.
ety: Clipping of balanced–unbalanced. Compare modem.
examples: In (e) a balun at the end of the coaxial feedline provides equal and opposite voltages to each side of the dipole and eliminates any current from the outside of the feedline.

senses: Wearing a gown.
ety: From gown + -ed.
examples: Deliberately, almost ‘augustly,’ the gowned and mortar-boarded figures followed one another through the great red turnstile and filed into the chamber beyond.
Pirates, buccaneers, the gowned ladies of the ancient pastoral – all the traditional subjects of imperial history – are among the images that take shape.
